Title: Your Agent Is Confidently Wrong: Guardrails for Agentic AI in Real Engineering Work
Abstract: Most agentic AI talks show the demo that worked. This one shows the ones that didn't, and what I changed after.  I am a Principal Engineer in Microsoft Fabric, where I am the tech lead and architect for capacity management. For the past year I have run AI agents against my actual job: incident triage, digging through telemetry, code review, and multi-step operational runbooks on a live multi-tenant platform. This talk is what I learned about trusting what they give back.  The capability is real. The failure modes are too, and they are not the ones the demos prepare you for. An agent hands you a number with no source and it reads like arithmetic. It cites documents that do not exist. One wrong fact spreads into every artifact it touches, and then it argues with you when you challenge it. Long sessions drift away from the facts. None of it looks like an error. It looks like a confident, well-formatted answer, and that is exactly what makes it expensive to catch.  This talk is about the discipline that makes agents safe to keep using. Force sources inline, so a claim with no source cannot survive. Verify before recommending, not after. Make the agent write its corrections down where you can see them. Keep "submitted" and "confirmed" as separate states in anything an agent tracks, because an agent will collapse them.  I will go through what I ended up with, the guardrails that held up, and the ones I dropped. You will leave knowing how to tell whether your agent is working or just sounds like it is.

Title: You Can't Flip a Flag at Step 17: Progressive Rollout for Autonomous Agents
Abstract: Feature flags assume two things: that the unit of release is a code path, and that you can turn it off at any moment. Autonomous agents break both.  I build computer-use agents at Obin AI — models that read screens, operate real desktop and web software, and complete document and back-office workflows inside regulated financial institutions. Shipping a change to one of these is not shipping a code path. It is granting a capability: the agent may now click Submit itself instead of stopping for a human. And you cannot revoke that mid-flight, because at step 17 of a 30-step workflow the agent has already mutated state in someone else's system.  This talk is the flag design we ended up with, and why the obvious version failed.  Rollout dimensions that turned out to matter, in order: autonomy level (suggest → draft → execute-with-review → execute unattended) is the axis that actually maps to risk, not percentage-of-traffic; per-tool grants, so blast radius is bounded by which tools the flag opens rather than by the agent's judgment; per-workflow rather than per-user, because the risk lives in the task, not the person; and per-tenant, because one institution's appetite is not another's.  Flag evaluation inside a long episode. Flags must be pinned at episode start and carried through, not re-read per step — otherwise the agent's behaviour changes underneath itself, and worse, you can no longer reconstruct months later why it did what it did. That reconstruction is an audit requirement, so the flag snapshot becomes part of the trace.  Kill switches that are actually safe. A hard stop mid-trajectory can leave a workflow half-applied. I will cover designing a drain state instead: refuse new episodes, let in-flight ones reach the next verifiable checkpoint, and stop there.  And measuring the rollout when the metric is cost per completed task and outcomes arrive hours later — which makes conventional percentage ramps close to useless.  Takeaways: an autonomy-level flag taxonomy, why to pin flags per-episode, and a drain-based kill switch design.

Title: Your AI Kill Switch Is Probably Broken
Abstract: Your autonomous agent starts making the wrong production calls.  You flip the kill switch.  The dashboard says Disabled.  Thirty seconds later, tool calls are still being executed.  Why?  Because changing a feature flag can stop new work without terminating work that is already in flight.  Most feature flags are admission controls. A real kill switch also needs cancellation semantics.  Feature flags are increasingly being used to control models, prompts, tools, routing, and agent behaviour at runtime. But autonomous systems introduce failure modes that ordinary feature toggles were never designed to solve: active tool executions that never re-evaluate the flag, stale provider state during connectivity failures, asynchronous workers operating from cached configuration, and fallback paths that have not seen production traffic in months.  In this 15-minute lightning talk, I will stage an automated Kill-Switch Fire Drill against a running agent loop and show three things:  1. The Admission-Control Trap: why disabling the flag blocks new agent runs while existing executions continue. 2. The Stale-State Trap: how cached state and provider failover can leave different workers with different views of whether the agent is actually enabled. 3. The Containment Proof: how to combine flag-evaluation events with OpenTelemetry and assert that active runs and tool calls reach zero within a defined containment SLO.  We will encode the expected behaviour in a small machine-readable Kill-Switch Contract, then deliberately flip the flag and prove whether the system actually obeys it.  I will also show the failure modes teams usually discover too late: fail-open defaults, stale fallback paths, partial shutdown, and an agent that still has access to the same control plane intended to contain it.  The takeaway is simple:  A flag value is intent. Containment is something you have to prove.  If your kill switch has never been exercised, do not wait for an AI incident to discover what it really switches off.

Title: Feature-Flagged Autonomy: Confidence-Gated Human-AI Logistics Systems
Abstract: As organizations adopt agentic AI, a key challenge is introducing autonomous decision-making safely while maintaining governance, compliance, and human oversight. This session presents a cloud-native framework for autonomous logistics that combines confidence-gated Human-in-the-Loop collaboration with feature-flag-driven operational control, enabling teams to deploy autonomous capabilities incrementally rather than through high-risk, all-or-nothing transitions.  The architecture integrates serverless infrastructure, edge computing for safety-critical decisions, multi-agent reinforcement learning, and a governance-first control layer. At its core is a dynamic decision-routing mechanism that assigns authority between AI agents and human operators based on real-time confidence evaluation instead of static rules. Feature flags are used to progressively enable, test, monitor, and roll back autonomous behaviors across operational workflows, providing a practical mechanism for reducing deployment risk while maintaining operational continuity.  The session explores architectural decisions, implementation patterns, and governance controls that support safe rollout of agentic systems in production environments. It addresses two common enterprise challenges: unreliable autonomous decisions in unfamiliar conditions and the emergence of ungoverned "shadow AI" systems operating outside established compliance frameworks. The framework incorporates policy enforcement, auditability, controlled system interaction, and decision monitoring directly into the operational workflow.  Attendees will learn how confidence-based decision routing and feature-flag strategies can work together to govern autonomous systems, improve operational resilience, and maintain trust in human-AI collaboration. The talk also provides a practical roadmap for organizations seeking to evolve from fragmented digital operations to governed autonomous systems while balancing innovation, compliance, and business risk.  Key takeaways include practical approaches for progressive rollout of AI capabilities, governance patterns for agentic systems, and lessons for managing autonomy in complex, real-world operational environments.

Title: Flagging the Black Box: Shipping AI Agents Safely with Feature Flags
Abstract: AI agents are non-deterministic, expensive, and occasionally confidently wrong—so how do you ship one to production without holding your breath? The answer turns out to be a tool we already trust: feature flags. This talk shows how I used flags to tame an agentic RAG system in production—gating the agent behind a kill switch, rolling it out to 1% of traffic, A/B testing a new retrieval strategy against the old one, and instantly reverting a bad prompt without a redeploy. We'll go concept by concept: flagging individual agent capabilities (retrieval, self-correction, tool use), using flags as runtime guardrails to cap cost and loop iterations, and running controlled experiments to prove a model change actually helped before rolling it everywhere. You'll see the flag architecture, the rollout strategy, and what broke when we got it wrong. If you're shipping anything powered by LLMs or agents, you'll leave knowing how to put a safety harness on it using infrastructure you probably already have. What Attendees Will Learn  Why non-deterministic AI systems need flags more than traditional features do How to gate agent capabilities behind flags—kill switches, gradual rollout, instant rollback Using flags as runtime guardrails to cap agent cost, retries, and loop iterations Running A/B experiments to validate a prompt or model change before full rollout A practical flag architecture for AI features you can adapt to your own stack

Title: The Agent Enablement Platform Is a Fleet of Disposable Computers
Abstract: Platform teams enabling coding agents across an org need repository-defined environments, leaseable isolated computers, warm pools, snapshot and fork, stable identity, scoped secrets, controlled networking, checkpoints, and real cleanup. This talk is built from what actually failed running that in practice, not theory. You leave with a concrete architecture for agent enablement that a platform team can operate, not just a demo.

Title: Feature-Flagging Data Governance: A Progressive Rollout Framework for Master Data Management at Scale
Abstract: Master Data Management initiatives often fail not from bad architecture but from all-or-nothing rollouts: a new governance rule, quality check, or matching algorithm goes live enterprise-wide and breaks downstream systems before anyone can react. This session reframes MDM as a progressive delivery problem, applying feature flag patterns to the rollout of data governance itself.  We walk through a practical framework for flagging MDM changes — canary-testing new data quality rules against a single business unit before global rollout, using kill switches to instantly revert a bad matching or standardization rule without a full redeploy, and gating AI-driven enrichment or deduplication logic behind cohort-based flags tied to data domain, region, or system of record. This lets governance teams ship changes with the same safety net application teams expect from progressive delivery, turning MDM rollouts into controlled, observable experiments rather than high-stakes big-bang releases.  Attendees will leave with concrete patterns for: flag-gating data quality and standardization rules, phased rollout strategies for master data changes across business domains, monitoring signals that indicate when to roll forward vs. roll back, and how this approach reduces reconciliation effort and manual error while giving governance teams the same agility and blast-radius control that feature flags bring to software releases.

Title: When a Feature Flag Changes a KPI: Managing Analytics Logic Safely
Abstract: Feature flags are commonly used to change application functionality, but what happens when the flagged behavior changes the data behind an important KPI? A seemingly small change in business logic can alter dashboards, reports, alerts, and executive metrics. This talk explores how data teams can treat analytics logic as a controlled deployment, using feature flags to introduce new calculations while comparing results against existing definitions. We will discuss metric versioning, reconciliation, data lineage, dashboard validation, and communicating changes to downstream consumers.

Title: Feature-Flagged Zero Trust: Safely Evolving Identity Controls in Cloud Systems
Abstract: Modern cloud environments require security controls to evolve continuously, but changes to identity policies, authentication flows, and authorization rules can introduce significant operational risk if deployed all at once. This session explores how feature flags can support the gradual rollout of Zero Trust and Identity Governance capabilities across cloud-first enterprises. Rather than treating identity controls as static policy, the approach combines continuous validation, adaptive access decisions, and controlled feature exposure to make security changes safer and easier to operate. The session examines practical patterns for introducing stronger authentication requirements, contextual access policies, Identity Threat Detection and Response capabilities, and automated governance workflows behind feature flags. Attendees will see how staged rollouts, targeted user cohorts, kill switches, telemetry, and rollback strategies can reduce disruption while security teams validate the impact of new controls in production. The talk also covers lessons around observability, policy testing, exception handling, and coordination between security and platform teams. Participants will leave with a practical architecture for using feature flags as an operational layer for evolving identity-centric security, enabling organizations to strengthen Zero Trust controls while maintaining reliability, developer velocity, and a predictable user experience.

Title: Feature Flags as the Configuration Layer for Multi-Tenant Workflow Behavior in Advertising and Financial Platforms
Abstract: Platforms serving hundreds of tenants face a core tension: every tenant needs different workflow behavior, but shipping code changes per tenant doesn't scale. This session shows how feature flags — not branching, not tenant-specific deploys — become the primary lever for controlling which workflow steps run, which thresholds apply, which external systems get called, and which roles can override a decision, all without a redeploy.  We'll walk through a four-dimension model — workflow graphs, data contracts, policies and routing, and isolation and limits — and show where flags sit inside each: enabling or disabling steps in impression/click attribution and billing pipelines, gating budget-and-pacing control loops for ad campaigns, and toggling enrichment, validation, and settlement paths for trade capture and compliance review workflows in financial services.  The talk covers practical flag implementation across two runtime patterns: short-lived, event-driven flows on serverless workflow engines (using the CNCF Serverless Workflow spec) versus long-running, human-in-the-loop processes on Temporal and Cadence  and why flag evaluation strategy differs between the two. We'll dig into the operational hard parts specific to flags at this scale: safely evolving flag schemas without breaking tenants mid-rollout, testing strategies that simulate hundreds of tenant-specific flag configurations realistically, and observability that separates platform-wide flag health from per-tenant flag behavior to catch noisy-neighbor effects and fairness issues before they escalate.  Attendees will leave with a concrete pattern for using flags as a tenant-isolation and progressive-rollout mechanism in regulated, high-stakes domains  applicable anywhere a platform needs to change behavior per customer without touching the codebase.

Title: Feature Flags as a Migration Engine: De-risking Domain-Driven Decomposition of Monolithic Payment Platforms
Abstract: Enterprise payment platforms have traditionally been built as monolithic systems to provide centralized deployment, dependable transactional behavior, and strong operational control. While these systems have successfully supported years of business growth, merchant onboarding, and product expansion, they become increasingly difficult to evolve as organizations introduce new payment methods, digital wallets, loyalty programs, hosted checkout solutions, and regional compliance requirements. This presentation explores how feature flags enable a safer, incremental path through Domain-Driven Decomposition, allowing teams to modernize these complex platforms around business capabilities rather than technical convenience without exposing the business to all-or-nothing cutover risk.  The session examines how Domain-Driven Design (DDD) defines bounded contexts across payment domains such as authorization, settlement, dispute handling, loyalty, and reporting, and how flags allow teams to route traffic between old and new implementations while these boundaries are validated in production. It discusses how ubiquitous language and context mapping help identify hidden dependencies and domain ownership, with flag-controlled rollouts providing a mechanism to test these boundaries against real transaction volume before committing fully.  The presentation introduces a taxonomy of migration patterns built around feature flagging as the control layer, including the Strangler Fig Pattern, Anti-Corruption Layer, and Branch by Abstraction, the last of which depends directly on toggles to switch between legacy and new code paths during active development. It presents a practical framework for sequencing extraction based on domain clarity, data ownership, operational criticality, and organizational readiness, with flag-based kill switches offering a fast rollback path if a newly extracted service misbehaves under production load.  Finally, the session discusses common challenges such as false decomposition, shared-database dependencies, over-fragmentation, and organizational alignment influenced by Conway's Law, along with the discipline required to manage flag lifecycle and technical debt as migrations progress. Attendees will gain practical insights into using feature flags to plan safer, reversible domain-driven modernization strategies that improve maintainability, service ownership, and long-term architectural evolution in enterprise payment platforms.

JobTitle1: Associate CRM Strategy and Operations Director
Title: De-Risking a Legacy CRM Migration in Life Sciences: Feature-Flag-Driven Rollout Strategy for a Governed Salesforce Patient Engagement Platform
Abstract: United Therapeutics needed to retire Keystone Entrada, a legacy patient CRM, and cut over patient communications to a new Salesforce-based ecosystem spanning Marketing Cloud, Data Cloud, and Health Cloud  without disrupting live patient engagement or risking PHI/PII exposure during the transition. A big-bang cutover was not an option given the compliance stakes and the volume of active patient touchpoints running through the legacy system.  This session shares how feature-flag-driven rollout strategy was used to control the blast radius of the migration: gating identity resolution and data unification behind flags as each source system was onboarded, toggling segmentation and activation logic into Marketing Cloud incrementally rather than all at once, and running the old and new HUB/copay ingestion pipelines in parallel behind flags to validate data integrity before fully retiring the legacy path.  Attendees will learn how progressive rollout patterns applied to a regulated, PHI-sensitive environment reduced the risk of duplicate records and broken personalization mid-migration, how flag-gated cutover supported governed, auditable rollback points at each stage, and how this approach let the team validate campaign performance and triggered communications on the new platform before fully decommissioning vendor dependencies. The talk translates feature-flag migration patterns more commonly seen in pure engineering contexts into a regulated, patient-data-heavy environment where governance and auditability carry as much weight as rollout speed.

Title: Dependency-Aware Upgrade Sequencing for Safe Modernization
Abstract: Modern enterprise software ecosystems often contain hundreds or thousands of interconnected services, libraries, APIs, messaging systems, and data platforms. In these environments, upgrading a single component can trigger compatibility issues, deployment failures, service outages, or unexpected security exposure across dependent systems. While automated dependency management tools accelerate updates, they frequently recommend isolated library upgrades without accounting for transitive dependencies and ecosystem-wide compatibility.  This session presents Dependency-Aware Topological Upgrade Sequencing, a practical approach for planning and executing upgrades across complex software environments. Using dependency graph analysis and topological sorting, teams can identify safe upgrade paths and establish clear "happens-before" relationships that ensure prerequisite components are upgraded before dependent services.  Attendees will learn how machine-readable dependency registries, service dependency graphs, and topology-driven planning can improve upgrade reliability and reduce operational risk. The session reviews real-world industry approaches, including Grandprix's topology-based upgrade ordering, Broadcom Tanzu Platform Upgrade Planner's dependency mapping capabilities, Kubernetes Cluster API's chained upgrade model for multi-version transitions, and CoreStory's dependency-driven modernization framework.  The talk also examines emerging innovations such as the UPCY project's graph-based compatibility optimization techniques and IBM's dependency-based software upgrade patent (US12182560B2). In addition, it explores how feature flags and progressive delivery practices can complement dependency-aware planning by enabling controlled rollouts, validation of upgraded services, and safer adoption of infrastructure and platform changes.  Participants will leave with practical techniques for mapping dependencies, assessing upgrade risk, prioritizing modernization efforts, and building repeatable upgrade workflows that improve visibility, reduce deployment friction, and support continuous modernization at scale.

Title: Configuration-Driven Canary Routing: Zero-Downtime API Migrations at High-Traffic Scale
Abstract: Feature flags are usually framed around toggling functionality on and off. But the same runtime-configuration principle, deciding behavior without a deployment, is what makes zero-downtime API protocol migrations possible at high-traffic scale.  I'll walk through configuration-driven canary routing patterns used to migrate a high-throughput microservice (processing thousands of requests per second) in a regulated financial services environment, where a bad rollout isn't just an inconvenience, it's a compliance incident. I'll cover how routing configuration controlled traffic shifting between protocol versions, what made rollback safe and fast, and the lessons learned running this in production.

Title: What Do You Flag When the Code Didn't Change?
Abstract: Your code hasn't changed. Your tests pass. Your deploy pipeline is idle. And your agent is behaving differently than it did last Tuesday, because a provider updated a model underneath you.  Feature flags were built for a world where the same code does the same thing every time. Agents break that assumption, and it turns out flags are one of the few controls that still work when the change you need to manage never went through your repository.

JobTitle1: Senior Staff Software Engineer, Enterprise Architecture and AI
Title: Eval-Gated Model Rollouts: Progressive Delivery for LLM Systems
Abstract: Swapping the model behind a production feature is a deploy, and most teams treat it like a config change. There is no canary, no rollback plan, and no measurement other than whether the endpoint still returns 200. Then someone routes 30 percent of traffic to a cheaper tier to cut the bill, quality drops in a way nobody is watching for, and it takes a week and a customer complaint to connect the two.  This talk applies progressive delivery to the nondeterministic part of the stack. The unit being flagged is not a code path, it is a model, a prompt version, or a retrieval strategy, and the thing gating the rollout is not a smoke test but an eval suite.  We cover the mechanics. Putting model selection behind a flag through a routing layer so a swap is a percentage change rather than a deploy. Canarying a model on a slice of traffic and comparing eval scores, cost per request, and latency side by side against the incumbent. Automatic rollback wired to eval score rather than to error rate, because a worse model does not error. Per-tenant and per-use-case targeting, so the cheap tier serves the workloads it can handle and the expensive one serves the rest. Shadow running a candidate against live traffic before it takes any real requests.  We also cover the discipline that makes cost work honest: every downgrade ships with the eval that justifies it, and the flag stays in place long enough to prove the saving held.  Takeaways: A flag-driven architecture for model routing. Canary and rollback criteria that work for nondeterministic systems. How to pair cost reduction with evidence instead of hope.  Audience: Platform engineers, AI engineers, and teams paying an LLM bill they want to cut safely. Level: Intermediate to advanced.

Title: Feature Flags for Safer Machine Learning Rollouts in Healthcare
Abstract: Machine learning is helping healthcare organizations improve clinical decision support, personalize treatment, detect diseases earlier, and streamline operations. However, deploying predictive models into real healthcare environments introduces significant risks. A model may perform well during testing but behave differently when exposed to new patient populations, changing data patterns, or complex clinical workflows.  This session explores how feature flags can help engineering and data teams release machine learning capabilities more safely across healthcare platforms. Attendees will learn how progressive rollouts, targeted activation, controlled experiments, and rapid rollback can reduce the risks associated with introducing new models and data-driven features.  The talk examines practical architecture patterns for separating model deployment from feature release, comparing new and existing models, testing integrations with electronic health records, and limiting exposure by hospital, user group, or workflow. It also covers monitoring model performance, detecting data-quality issues, validating clinical impact, and responding quickly when unexpected behavior occurs.  The session will discuss lessons learned from balancing scalability, reliability, privacy, HIPAA requirements, and patient trust. Attendees will leave with practical guidance for combining feature flags, scalable data platforms, observability, and machine learning workflows to deliver healthcare innovation with greater control and confidence.

Title: Feature Flags for Safer Machine Learning Credit Decisions and Controlled Model Rollouts
Abstract: Machine learning is increasingly used to support credit line assignment, risk segmentation, underwriting, and portfolio optimization. However, deploying changes to credit decisioning models can introduce significant operational, financial, and regulatory risk. A model update that performs well in testing may behave differently when exposed to real customer activity, changing market conditions, or previously unseen data patterns.  This session presents a practical framework for using feature flags to deploy and manage machine learning-driven credit line strategies more safely. It will explain how financial institutions can separate model deployment from model activation, gradually release new scoring logic, test updated segmentation approaches, and control access to experimental features without requiring repeated production deployments.  The presentation will cover progressive rollouts, cohort-based activation, champion–challenger testing, canary releases, kill switches, and controlled experimentation. It will also show how feature flags can support comparisons between existing credit policies and new machine learning models that use bureau variables, payment behavior, spending patterns, and credit utilization trends.  Attendees will learn how to connect feature-flag decisions with monitoring for model performance, approval rates, credit exposure, fairness, drift, and unexpected customer outcomes. The session will also discuss governance considerations, including audit trails, approval workflows, flag ownership, expiration policies, and emergency rollback procedures.  By combining feature flags with machine learning observability and model governance, teams can introduce credit decisioning changes incrementally, reduce deployment risk, and respond quickly when results deviate from expectations. This session is especially relevant for professionals working in financial technology, credit risk, data science, MLOps, platform engineering, feature management, and regulated software delivery.

JobTitle1: Senior Lead Technical AI Evaluation Specialist
Title: Beyond On/Off: Using Quality Gates to Safely Release GenAI Features
Abstract: Feature flags give engineering teams control over when software reaches users. But with Generative AI, controlling exposure is only part of the problem. A feature can be technically healthy while its answers become less accurate, grounded, safe, or performant.  In this talk, I’ll share an engineering approach for combining feature flags, automated AI evaluation, and quality gates to make GenAI releases safer and more measurable. Instead of treating evaluation as a manual exercise performed shortly before release, teams can continuously evaluate model and application behavior and use those signals to inform rollout decisions.  We’ll look at how automated evaluation pipelines can measure answer quality, grounding, safety, latency, and regression against established baselines; how quality thresholds can become release criteria; and how progressive rollout and feature flags provide a practical control plane when AI behavior changes unexpectedly.  Attendees will leave with a reusable pattern for moving from “is the feature enabled?” to “has the feature demonstrated that it is ready to be enabled?”

Title: Feature Flag–Driven API Resilience Through Autonomous Monitoring and Auto-Healing
Abstract: Modern microservices environments depend on APIs for critical service-to-service communication, making reliability, recovery speed, and operational control essential. This session presents a practical approach to building resilient API platforms by combining continuous health monitoring, automated recovery workflows, adaptive scaling, and feature flag–driven operational controls.  The talk explores an intelligent API health management framework that continuously monitors service endpoints, detects anomalies in real time, and initiates automated recovery actions with minimal human intervention. When degradation or failures occur, the system can redirect traffic, restart affected services, and adjust resource allocation to maintain service availability and performance.  A key focus is how feature flags extend beyond application releases and become an operational tool for reliability engineering. Feature flags enable teams to progressively roll out functionality, isolate problematic features, perform targeted rollbacks, and reduce the blast radius of failures without requiring full deployments. The session demonstrates how feature flags work alongside observability platforms, cloud-native orchestration, and automated failover mechanisms to improve system resilience in production environments.  In addition to the architecture, the talk shares practical lessons learned from implementing automated monitoring and recovery pipelines, including operational challenges, dependency management considerations, and trade-offs encountered while building self-healing systems. Attendees will also see measurable outcomes such as reduced service disruption, faster recovery cycles, and more efficient infrastructure utilization under changing workloads.  Participants will leave with actionable patterns for integrating feature flags into reliability workflows, designing self-healing API platforms, and improving operational resilience through automation, observability, and adaptive scaling.  This session is intended for platform engineers, SREs, architects, and engineering leaders responsible for building and operating reliable cloud-native systems.

Title: Your Kill Switch Is Untested and You Will Find Out at 3am
Abstract: Most teams treat the ability to turn something off as the safety net that makes everything else acceptable. Ship fast, we can always flip it back. I believed that too, until the night I tried to undo something an agent had written and found that undoing it did not work either.  The change touched more than I thought, in ways that were individually reasonable, and reversing it turned out to be a careful manual unwind rather than one switch. That is a bad thing to learn while a service is down, and it is the specific reason I stopped accepting "we can always turn it off" as a reason to let an agent ship something unbounded.  Since then I have treated the reverse path as something that has to be tested on purpose, the same way you would test anything else you depend on in an emergency. This talk is how I do that. How I bound a change so that reversing it is genuinely one action rather than a sequence. How I verify the reverse actually runs instead of assuming it will. And what I found once I started deliberately breaking things to see whether recovery behaved the way I expected.  I will be honest about the cost, because this slows you down. The useful question is not whether to do it but which changes deserve it, and I will tell you where I draw that line and why.  For anyone whose kill switch has never been pulled in anger.

Title: One flag, no deploy: switching diagnostics and providers at runtime in a one-person production app
Abstract: I run two production web apps alone. When something goes wrong at eleven at night I cannot ship a build with more logging and wait. So the diagnostics live behind a flag in Cloudflare KV: off, admin only, or everyone, flipped in seconds and read on every request. The same shape controls the writer: after four consecutive failures from the primary language-model provider the app hands off to a second provider on another cloud, and the flag tells me when it did. This talk is the small, boring machinery of that: how the flag is read without adding latency, what the "admin only" state is for and what it costs, why the failover threshold is four and not one, and a deliberate failover test, forced on purpose on 24 September 2026 with the trace switched on, what it recorded, and what I changed after. Nothing here needs a platform team. It needs one key in a KV store and the discipline to leave the switch off.  **Outline**, pre-recorded, 25 to 30 minutes. 1. The app and the constraint: one engineer, two products, no on-call rota but me. 2. The trace flag: three states in KV, how each request reads it, what each state logs, the cost of leaving it on. 3. The admin-only state: raising diagnostics for one account while every other user sees nothing. 4. The writer failover as a flag: the four-failure trigger, the second provider, what the flag records on handoff. 5. The deliberate test of 24 September 2026: forcing the trigger, the timeline, the output quality on the fallback, what changed. 6. Rules I keep: flags are read, never cached past a request. Every flip is dated in a file. The switch goes off when the work is done.  **Takeaways.** A three-state flag (off, admin, all) is worth more than a boolean for diagnostics. Read flags per request from a store built for it and the latency is nothing. A provider failover is a flag with a counter. Test the failover on purpose before it tests you. Turn it off when you are done, and write down that you did.

Title: Feature Flags as Incident Evidence: Safer AI-Assisted RCA Workflows
Abstract: AI agents can make incident response faster. Without governance, they can also make the wrong response faster.  This talk starts in the middle of a production incident: the alert is clear, but the next safe decision is not. Metrics are in one system, logs in another, feature flags somewhere else, a deployment landed recently, and the runbook may be stale. The on-call engineer is not slow; they are assembling decision context across too many systems under pressure.  Beacon is a governed decision-control plane for AI-assisted incident response. Instead of starting with an open-ended chatbot, Beacon turns an alert into a workflow: evidence intake, ranked hypotheses, explicit operator decision, scoped follow-up, and traceability throughout. The model is a reasoning component over structured facts. It does not own the incident workflow, merge changes, promote deploys, or bypass approval.  We will walk through the architecture patterns that make this boundary credible for teams that use feature flags as release controls, incident evidence, rollback candidates, and policy gates: typed evidence from metrics, logs, feature flags, Kubernetes context, and repository history; service-bounded retrieval for runbooks and architecture notes; confidence as a workflow signal rather than production authority; policy gates before action; and post-incident artifacts that preserve what the agent knew, what policy allowed, and who made the decision.  Attendees will leave with a practical mental model for production-minded AI agents: evidence first, reasoning second, operator decision third, and an audit trail that survives the chat window.

Title: Self-Optimizing Infrastructure: Putting AI Inside the SDLC at 200K Requests per Second
Abstract: Most teams treat AI in operations as a dashboard — something a human checks after the damage is done. At the scale of a connected-device fleet serving 200,000+ requests per second across tens of thousands of servers, that model has already failed: the operational data outpaces human analysis, and a quiet 15% CPU regression in a hot-path API becomes a fleet-sized capacity bill before anyone opens a graph.  This session makes the case for AI as an operator rather than an observer, and walks through the closed loop that makes it work: performance-aware code review at development time, payload replay and resource-signature profiling in CI, phased canary→cell→region deployment, baseline-learned anomaly detection that correlates a code or payload change to a CPU/memory/IO spike, and a remediation agent that proposes and applies a fix — then re-proves it through the same phased pipeline before the system trusts it.  We'll cover the guardrails that make autonomous action safe in production: contained blast radius, reversibility, logged and reviewable actions, and where the human stays in the loop for high-stakes calls. Drawn from running service operations for a large-scale consumer IoT platform, where reliability isn't an SLA credit — it's whether the camera at someone's front door is working.

Title: Building Self-Healing Cloud Infrastructure with Feature Flags
Abstract: Modern cloud infrastructure must remain reliable when services fail, workloads become unstable, dependencies behave unpredictably, or newly introduced changes create operational risk. This session presents a practical approach to building self-healing cloud systems using four core practices: automated failure detection, automated recovery, blast-radius reduction, and operational resilience.  The talk explores how feature flags can support these practices by giving infrastructure teams greater control over how changes are activated, monitored, limited, and reversed. Attendees will learn how teams can use feature flags to gradually enable infrastructure behavior, deactivate unstable functionality, isolate affected workloads, and support faster recovery when monitoring systems detect unexpected conditions.  The session also examines how automated detection and recovery mechanisms can reduce reliance on manual intervention. By combining health signals, recovery workflows, and controlled feature activation, teams can respond more consistently to service disruptions while minimizing the impact on dependent systems.  A key focus will be limiting the blast radius of failures. Feature flags can help restrict changes to selected services, workloads, clusters, or environments, preventing one localized issue from becoming a wider platform disruption.  Designed for cloud engineers, DevOps professionals, SREs, platform engineers, and infrastructure architects, this session provides practical architectural guidance for building cloud systems that detect problems, recover automatically, contain failures, and remain manageable during operational change.

Title: Beyond On and Off: Using Feature Flags for Safer Cloud Deployments
Abstract: Feature flags are often viewed as simple on-and-off switches, but in modern software delivery they have become powerful tools for reducing deployment risk and improving release strategies. When used effectively, feature flags help teams separate deployment from release, experiment safely, and gain greater control over system behavior.  In this session, I’ll explore how feature flags can be integrated into modern cloud and DevOps workflows to support safer deployments and operational flexibility. We’ll discuss progressive rollouts, canary releases, controlled experimentation, rollback strategies, and practical implementation considerations.  The talk will also cover common mistakes teams make when managing feature flags, including technical debt, complexity growth, and governance challenges. Attendees will leave with practical guidance on using feature flags as part of reliable and scalable software delivery practices.  Whether you are introducing feature flags for the first time or refining an existing approach, this session provides practical lessons that can be applied immediately.

Title: Guardrails That Outlive the Rollout: Adaptive Statistical Risk Control for Feature Flags
Abstract: Guardrail metrics are usually built for one rollout shape — a fixed percentage, a fixed segment. But targeting rules change mid-flight: a flag expands to new cohorts, a canary widens, an experiment's exposure shifts after the guardrail was already calibrated. This session asks whether adaptive statistical bounds can stay valid across that kind of drift, without being re-derived every time a rollout configuration changes.  Using a rigorous, multi-decade financial dataset as a stress-test proxy — U.S. Treasury yield data, chosen for its long out-of-sample history and well-documented regime shifts — the study compares static (Gaussian) bounds, rolling recalibration, adaptive conformal methods, and bounds calibrated to a fixed, predefined set of exposure scenarios. Each approach is scored not just on average accuracy but on whether its misses cluster in time — the same failure mode that turns a guardrail from "safe" into "quietly broken" during a bad rollout window.  The results show a real tradeoff. A single guardrail built to cover every possible exposure shape closes the average-accuracy gap but still produces clustered failures during regime change — false confidence at exactly the moment a rollout is riskiest. A guardrail scoped to a known, bounded set of exposure scenarios is tighter and more reliable within that scope, but breaks its guarantee the moment a genuinely new configuration appears. The talk lands on a practical two-layer architecture: a broad, reusable guardrail for exposures you haven't anticipated, paired with a narrower, sharper guardrail for exposures you have. Attendees leave with a concrete framework for deciding when a guardrail can be trusted to generalize — and when it needs to be re-scoped as flags evolve.

Title: Progressive OS Rollouts: Engineering Safe Updates Beyond Feature Flags
Abstract: Feature flags have transformed how applications are released by enabling gradual rollouts, rapid rollback, and controlled experimentation. Operating system updates face many of the same challenges, but with significantly higher stakes. A failed rollout can leave devices in an unrecoverable state, making dependency management and recovery design essential rather than optional.  This session explores how the principles behind progressive delivery can be applied to silent OTA updates for connected devices. It explains why linear update sequences are fragile, how dependency graphs provide a safer execution model, and why validating update relationships before deployment is critical to reliable releases. The talk also examines resumable execution, rollback boundaries, and verification checkpoints that allow updates to recover safely from interruptions without requiring user intervention.  Rather than focusing solely on deployment success, the session discusses operational measures such as recovery time, user-visible disruption, and recovery rate to better understand rollout quality in production. Attendees will see how release engineering concepts extend beyond application feature flags into the operating system layer, where safe sequencing and controlled recovery determine whether large-scale deployments succeed.

Title: Using Feature Flags to Improve HR Technology Delivery
Abstract: Modern HR platforms support critical employee lifecycle processes, including recruitment, onboarding, payroll, benefits, performance management, employee self-service, and offboarding. Releasing changes across these interconnected systems can be risky because even a small defect may affect employee experience, data accuracy, compliance, or essential HR operations.  This session explores how feature flags can help HR technology teams ship changes more safely and continuously. Attendees will learn how to use controlled rollouts to introduce new HRIS capabilities to selected users, departments, regions, or employee groups before expanding them across the organization.  The talk examines practical applications in recruitment workflows, self-service portals, payroll processes, analytics features, personalized employee journeys, and system integrations. It also explains how feature flags can support testing in production, faster incident response, controlled experimentation, and rapid feature deactivation when unexpected issues occur.  Key engineering considerations include flag design, ownership, access control, monitoring, observability, testing, documentation, and cleanup. The session also addresses common mistakes such as long-lived flags, overlapping conditions, limited visibility, and insufficient governance.  Attendees will leave with actionable practices for building a maintainable feature flag workflow that reduces release risk, improves system reliability, and enables continuous enhancement of HR technology without disrupting critical employee services.
